opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think about it mostly in terms of how much context I already have in my head and how well-specified the task is.

When I'm in the middle of something, actively thinking through a design, making lots of small decisions, and I want to stay in the loop on every line, the IDE-style tools are great. Autocomplete, inline edits, "rewrite this function," "explain this block." I'm still the one driving, and the AI just shortens the distance between what I'm thinking and what ends up on the screen. The feedback loop is seconds, and that matters for that kind of exploratory work.

Agentic tools shine when I can describe the outcome more easily than the steps. "Add tests for this module." "Migrate these call sites to the new API." "Figure out why this build is failing and fix it." Those tasks span many files, involve running things and reacting to the output, and I don't really need to watch every keystroke. I need to check the result. So I hand it off, go do something else, and come back to review a diff.

A heuristic I use: if reviewing the output is much cheaper than producing it, and there's a good way to verify it, like tests, a type checker, or a clear spec, that's a strong signal for an agent. If the work is really about me figuring out what I want, and the code is almost a byproduct of my thinking, I want to stay close to it in the editor.

The line keeps moving, though. As the agents get more reliable over longer horizons, more of what used to be "I'd better do this myself" becomes "I can delegate this and review it." So a lot of the skill now is learning to scope and specify work well enough to hand it off, which is a different muscle from writing the code yourself.

r001.rationale: It says IDE tools let the developer stay in the loop while shortening the path from thought to code, preserving the flow of active coding.

r002.rationale: It gives agentic tools examples such as adding tests, migrating call sites, and fixing a build, but does not identify de novo development as especially well suited to them.

r003.rationale: It says the developer can hand off multi-file tasks, do something else, and return to review the result.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think about it mostly in terms of how well-specified the task is and how much I actually need to be in the loop while it's happening.

The IDE-style stuff, the autocomplete and the inline chat, that's great when I'm already in the code and I know exactly what I want to write. I'm just moving faster. The context is right there, I can see the suggestion, I can accept it or not in half a second, and the cost of a bad suggestion is basically zero because I'm reading every line anyway. It's a very tight feedback loop, and it works because I'm still the one holding the plan in my head.

The agentic tools are a different mode. There I'm handing off a chunk of work and walking away from it, or at least stepping back from it. So the things that go well are tasks where I can describe the outcome clearly and there's some way to check whether it's right. Write this migration, add tests for this module, go fix the type errors in this package, wire up this endpoint the way these three other endpoints are done. Things that are kind of tedious and spread across a bunch of files, but where there's a pattern to follow. That's where I get the biggest multiplier, because the agent can go read the codebase, make the changes, run the tests, and iterate without me babysitting each step.

Where the agentic tools tend to fall down for me is when the task is really a design question in disguise. If I don't actually know what I want yet, and I'm figuring it out by writing the code, then delegating that is sort of a mistake. The agent will make a bunch of decisions, and they'll be plausible, and then I'll spend more time understanding and unwinding them than I would have spent just doing it. So for exploratory work, or anything where the architecture is still fluid, I want to be in the editor, using the lighter-weight assistance.

The other dimension is verification. If I can't easily tell whether the result is right, I'm much more hesitant to hand it off. Good tests, a type checker, a clear spec, those all make agentic work feel safe. Without them, I'm basically trusting the model, and I've been burned enough times to know that's not a great idea yet.

So the rough heuristic is: well-specified and verifiable, hand it to the agent. Fuzzy or design-heavy, stay in the IDE and let the model help me think faster rather than think for me. And honestly the boundary keeps moving. Things I wouldn't have delegated a year ago, I delegate without thinking about it now.

r001.rationale: The response says IDE assistance helps when the developer is already coding and keeps a tight feedback loop, letting them move faster while staying in control.

r002.rationale: It describes agentic tools as useful for clearly specified tasks that follow existing patterns, but does not identify de novo development work as particularly well suited to them.

r003.rationale: It describes handing off a chunk of work and stepping away while the agent works across files, which conveys delegating work outside the developer’s immediate focus.

astra-6.text:
I think about it in terms of how well I can specify the task and how quickly I can tell whether the result is right. If I can say, “Here’s the bug, here’s how to reproduce it, and here’s the test that should pass,” that’s a good candidate for handing off to an agent. It can explore the codebase, make changes, and come back with something I can review.

If I’m still figuring out what I want to build, I tend to want a tighter loop. I’m writing a little code, looking at what happens, and changing my mind about the design. That’s where AI functionality in the IDE is useful, because I’m driving and it’s helping me move faster.

So it’s less about whether the task is big or small and more about whether I can delegate it with a clear definition of success. And those modes can happen within the same project: I might work interactively to figure out the approach, then hand off the more clearly defined pieces.

r001.rationale: It describes using IDE assistance in a tighter, interactive loop while the developer drives and changes the design, which conveys help maintaining coding flow.

r002.rationale: For work where the developer is still figuring out what to build, the response prefers IDE assistance; it reserves agent handoffs for clearly specified tasks.

r003.rationale: It describes handing a defined task to an agent, but does not identify delegating work outside the developer’s current focus as a useful application.

sol-6.1.text:
The distinction for me is how well I can specify the task up front and how quickly I can tell whether the result is correct. If I can say, “Here’s a bug, here’s how to reproduce it, and here’s the test that should pass,” that’s a great task to hand off to an agent. It can go explore the codebase, make changes, run tests, and come back with something I can review.

When I’m still figuring out what to build, I tend to want to be in the IDE. I’m looking at the code, trying out an abstraction, and changing my mind as I learn. In that setting, autocomplete and asking questions about the code are useful because they keep me moving without requiring me to articulate the whole task in advance.

So it’s less a distinction between easy and hard work, and more about how much of the direction I can delegate. Sometimes a fairly involved change is easy to hand off because the desired outcome is clear. And sometimes a small change requires a lot of back-and-forth because I haven’t decided what the right outcome is yet.

r001.rationale: The response says IDE autocomplete and code questions “keep me moving” while the developer is still exploring, identifying preserved coding flow as a benefit.

r002.rationale: The response says that when still figuring out what to build, the developer tends to want to work in the IDE; it does not identify de novo work as especially suited to agents.

r003.rationale: The response describes handing off well-specified tasks, but does not say that agents are useful for work outside the developer’s current focus.
